Chapter 6: Carrying the Torch—The Ongoing Fight for Justice
You know, the world doesn’t always move at the pace people need—especially for those who’ve suffered.
For Yazidi survivors, justice can feel like a distant light. Sometimes, it shines bright and hopeful. Other times, it flickers, barely visible, just out of reach. Their journey from being victims to finding their own power isn’t a straight road. Instead, it winds and twists—full of setbacks, moments of doubt, but also unexpected allies and those hard-won, little victories.
After the violence, these survivors find themselves facing a new kind of struggle. This time, the enemy isn’t someone with a weapon—it’s indifference, endless bureaucracy, and the slow, grinding gears of international law. Seeking justice is exhausting. There are forms to fill out, interviews to get through, and hearings where they’re asked to relive their most painful memories, again and again.
Some days, it probably feels like they’re just shouting into the wind.
Yet, even then, there are people who refuse to give up. Imagine a woman who once hid her face in fear, now sitting across from a panel of judges, her voice steady as she tells her story—not just for herself, but for everyone who can’t speak. That sense of responsibility weighs heavy, but it also gives her purpose.
And sometimes, the world does pay attention. International organizations start to document the crimes. A few of those responsible are brought to trial. When survivors watch these trials, they feel a mix of hope and skepticism. Justice, when it finally arrives, never feels complete. No verdict can bring back loved ones or erase those deep scars. Still, every conviction is a small step—a sign that the world hasn’t completely turned away.
Most of us will never know what it’s like to sit in a courtroom and relive our darkest moments in front of strangers. For the Yazidis, that’s just the cost of being heard. The process drags on, and the results often disappoint. But here’s something important: even just seeking justice—even refusing to stay silent—is a kind of healing. It’s a way to reclaim dignity, to say, “What happened matters.”
In quieter moments, survivors come together to share updates—news about the latest developments. There’s a lot of frustration, but also this stubborn hope that refuses to die. Because in the end, the fight for justice isn’t only about punishment. It’s about being seen. It’s about making sure the world remembers, and that the truth is passed on to future generations.
The journey’s far from over. But the torch? It’s still being carried forward.
